subject: Biology
title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
summary: Molecular Basis of Inheritance follows the genetic material from its chemistry to its use: the structure and packaging of DNA, the experiments that proved DNA is the genetic material, replication, transcription, the genetic code, translation, the lac operon, the Human Genome Project and DNA fingerprinting. It is the longest and highest-yielding chapter of the Genetics and Evolution unit, and almost every board paper draws a 3-mark or 5-mark question from it.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 12 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper. This chapter sits in Unit VII, Genetics and Evolution, which carries 20 marks in the CBSE blueprint, shared with Principles of Inheritance and Variation and Evolution. Molecular Basis of Inheritance usually supplies the biggest share of that unit: one or two 1-mark items, a 2-mark, a 3-mark and very often a 5-mark or case-based question.

question_types.note: Chargaff-type percentage calculations, the enzyme or factor for a step (sigma, rho, ligase, RNA polymerase II), the number of codons, the initiator codon, the gene products of z, y and a, the probe used in fingerprinting, the scientist behind an experiment.
DNA versus RNA stability (2'-OH), leading versus lagging strand, only one strand is transcribed, lac operon as negative regulation, AUG as a dual-function codon, histones being positively charged.

Nucleosome structure; euchromatin versus heterochromatin; why hnRNA is spliced; dual role of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates; cistron versus exon; template versus coding strand; VNTR; why HGP is a mega project; charging of tRNA.

Meselson and Stahl; Hershey and Chase; Griffith plus Avery, MacLeod and McCarty; features of the genetic code; hnRNA processing; lac operon in presence and absence of lactose; steps of DNA fingerprinting; salient features of the human genome; construct a transcription unit from a given strand.

Replication with a labelled fork and the role of each enzyme; transcription in bacteria and how eukaryotes differ; translation in full; lac operon with a labelled diagram in the switched-off and switched-on states; the whole search for genetic material from Griffith to Hershey and Chase; DNA fingerprinting with a flow chart.

A Meselson–Stahl density-gradient picture, a replication-fork or transcription-unit diagram, a lac operon sketch, a DNA fingerprint gel for a paternity or crime case, or an mRNA-and-amino-acid sequence to test properties of the code.

hot_topics: DNA replication: semi-conservative proof (Meselson–Stahl), the fork, leading and lagging strands, DNA ligase, dNTPs as substrate and energy
Transcription in prokaryotes (sigma and rho) and the three extra complexities in eukaryotes (three polymerases, splicing, capping and tailing)
The search for genetic material: Griffith, Avery–MacLeod–McCarty, Hershey–Chase with <sup>32</sup>P and <sup>35</sup>S
Genetic code: 64 codons, degenerate, unambiguous, universal, AUG and the stop codons; Gamow, Nirenberg, Khorana, Ochoa
Lac operon: i, p, o, z, y, a; inducer, repressor, negative regulation; diagram in the switched-off state
DNA fingerprinting: VNTR, Southern blotting, autoradiography, applications
Structure and packaging of DNA: polynucleotide chain with polarity, double helix features, nucleosome, euchromatin and heterochromatin
Human Genome Project: goals, methods (ESTs and sequence annotation), BAC and YAC, salient features, SNPs

sections.heading: 5.1 The DNA
sections.body:
The chapter opens by fixing what DNA is, how long it is and how much of it a cell has to manage. DNA is a long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; RNA is a polymer of ribonucleotides. Nucleic acids were first isolated by Friedrich Meischer in 1869, who called the material nuclein. DNA in most organisms is the genetic material; in some viruses RNA does that job instead.

The length of a DNA molecule is stated as the number of nucleotides it holds, or the number of base pairs (bp) if it is double stranded. Learn the four NCERT figures, because 1-mark questions pick them out: bacteriophage φ×174 has 5386 nucleotides, bacteriophage lambda has 48,502 bp, Escherichia coli has 4.6 × 106 bp, and the haploid human genome has 3.3 × 109 bp.

The size problem becomes obvious once you convert base pairs into metres. Adjacent base pairs are 0.34 nm apart along the helix, so a diploid human cell, with 6.6 × 109 bp, carries about 6.6 × 109 × 0.34 × 10−9 m ≈ 2.2 m of DNA inside a nucleus around 10−6 m across. Even E. coli must fit about 1.36 mm of DNA (the figure NCERT quotes) in a cell far smaller than that. The packaging problem, and its solution (section 5.1.2), follows directly from this calculation, and examiners like a question that asks you to do it.

Everything else in the chapter builds on two questions: what is the chemical structure of this polymer, and how does a cell copy it, read it and control it. Keep the numbers above on your formula sheet; they cost nothing to learn and are asked as fill-ups and MCQs.

formulas.expr: Length of DNA = number of base pairs × 0.34 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
where: distance between adjacent base pairs along the helix

sections.tip: Quote the human genome as 3.3 × 10<sup>9</sup> bp (haploid) but use 6.6 × 10<sup>9</sup> bp when calculating the 2.2 m length of DNA in a diploid cell; mixing the two is a common half-mark loss.

sections.heading: 5.1.1 Structure of Polynucleotide Chain
sections.body:
A nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA, 2'-deoxyribose in DNA) and a phosphate group. The bases are of two kinds: purines (adenine A, guanine G, double-ringed) and pyrimidines (cytosine C, uracil U, thymine T, single-ringed). Cytosine is common to both nucleic acids; thymine is found in DNA and uracil in RNA. Thymine is 5-methyl uracil.

The linkages are asked by name, so learn them exactly. Base joined to the 1' carbon of the pentose through an N-glycosidic linkage gives a nucleoside (adenosine or deoxyadenosine, guanosine or deoxyguanosine, cytidine or deoxycytidine, uridine or deoxythymidine). A phosphate added to the 5'-OH of the nucleoside through a phosphoester linkage gives a nucleotide. Two nucleotides join through a 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage to form a dinucleotide, and many join to form a polynucleotide chain. Every chain therefore has a free phosphate at its 5' end and a free 3'-OH at its 3' end; the backbone is sugar-phosphate and the bases project out from it.

Watson and Crick (1953) proposed the double helix using the X-ray diffraction data of Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin and the base-ratio observation of Erwin Chargaff that in double-stranded DNA the ratios A : T and G : C are constant and equal to one. The salient features of the double helix, as the marking scheme lists them: (i) it is made of two polynucleotide chains whose backbone is sugar-phosphate and whose bases point inward; (ii) the two chains are antiparallel, one 5'→3' and the other 3'→5'; (iii) the bases of the two strands pair by hydrogen bonds, A with T through two hydrogen bonds and G with C through three, and a purine always faces a pyrimidine, which keeps the distance between the strands uniform; (iv) the chains coil in a right-handed fashion with a pitch of 3.4 nm and roughly 10 bp per turn, so adjacent base pairs are 0.34 nm apart; (v) the planes of stacked base pairs lie one over the other, and this stacking, along with hydrogen bonding, confers stability on the helix.

The double helix explained how genetic information could be copied, and from it Francis Crick proposed the central dogma: genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein. In some viruses the flow runs RNA → DNA, called reverse transcription.

formulas.expr: Base + pentose (N-glycosidic linkage) → nucleoside; nucleoside + phosphate at 5'-OH (phosphoester linkage) → nucleotide; nucleotide + nucleotide (3'-5' phosphodiester linkage) → dinucleotide
A = T (2 H-bonds), G ≡ C (3 H-bonds); A + G = T + C; A/T = G/C = 1
Pitch 3.4 nm; 10 bp per turn; 0.34 nm between adjacent base pairs
where: length of one complete turn of the helix

sections.tip: For a percentage question: if C = 20%, then G = 20%, so A + T = 60% and A = 30%. In any double-stranded DNA, purines equal pyrimidines, so 1000 nucleotides always hold 500 pyrimidines.

sections.heading: 5.1.2 Packaging of DNA Helix
sections.body:
The 2.2 m of DNA in a human cell and the 1.36 mm in E. coli must be folded into a very small space. Prokaryotes have no defined nucleus, yet their DNA is not scattered: the negatively charged DNA is held with some positively charged proteins in a region called the nucleoid, where it is organised into large loops.

Eukaryotes use histones. These are small basic proteins rich in the amino acids lysine and arginine, whose side chains are positively charged. Eight histone molecules (two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4) form a histone octamer. The negatively charged DNA winds around the positively charged octamer to make a nucleosome; a typical nucleosome carries about 200 bp of DNA helix. Histone H1 sits where DNA enters and leaves the core. Nucleosomes repeat along the DNA to give chromatin, the thread-like structure seen as beads-on-string under the electron microscope. The string is coiled further to form the chromatin fibre, which is condensed at metaphase into chromosomes. These higher levels of packaging need additional non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins.

In a typical nucleus some chromatin stains light and some dark. The loosely packed, lightly stained region is euchromatin; it is transcriptionally active. The densely packed, dark-staining region is heterochromatin; it is transcriptionally inactive. This distinction is a 2-mark regular.

The 2-mark questions on this section are almost formulaic: name the positively charged component (histone octamer) and the negatively charged one (DNA); name the two amino acids that give histones their charge (lysine, arginine); draw and label the nucleosome; explain why a prokaryote's DNA is not scattered although it has no nucleus.

formulas.expr: Histone octamer (2 × H2A, H2B, H3, H4) + ~200 bp DNA → nucleosome; nucleosomes on DNA → chromatin (beads-on-string)
where: linker histone at entry and exit of DNA
non-histone chromosomal proteins needed for higher-order packaging

sections.tip: Write euchromatin = loosely packed, light, active and heterochromatin = densely packed, dark, inactive in one line each; both halves of the contrast earn the marks.

sections.heading: 5.2 The Search for Genetic Material: Transforming Principle and its Biochemical Characterisation
sections.body:
By the 1920s chromosomes were known to carry genes, but chromosomes contain both DNA and protein, and protein looked like the better candidate. Two experiments settled the question, and the board asks both.

Griffith's experiment (1928). Frederick Griffith worked with Streptococcus pneumoniae, which causes pneumonia. On a culture plate some colonies are smooth (S) because the cells have a mucous polysaccharide coat, and some are rough (R) because they lack it. S cells are virulent and R cells are not. Injected into mice: live S → mouse dies; live R → mouse lives; heat-killed S → mouse lives; heat-killed S mixed with live R → mouse dies, and living S bacteria are recovered from the dead mouse. Griffith concluded that some transforming principle had passed from the heat-killed S cells to the R cells and enabled them to synthesise the smooth polysaccharide coat and become virulent. He did not know its chemical nature.

Biochemical characterisation: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933–44). They purified biochemicals (proteins, DNA, RNA) from heat-killed S cells to see which could transform live R cells into S cells. DNA alone transformed R cells. Proteases and RNases did not affect transformation, so the transforming substance was neither protein nor RNA. DNase inhibited transformation, showing that DNA caused the transformation. They concluded that DNA is the hereditary material, although not all biologists were convinced.

In an exam answer, structure it as: organism and the two strains, the four injections and their results, the conclusion, then the three enzyme treatments and their outcomes. A flow-chart question on Griffith carries 3 marks and wants the outcomes of each step written next to the arrows.

formulas.expr: Heat-killed S + live R → live S recovered (transformation); protease/RNase: no effect; DNase: transformation blocked

sections.tip: Griffith showed that transformation happens; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA does it. Give each group its own conclusion or the examiner deducts.

sections.heading: 5.2.1 The Genetic Material is DNA: Hershey and Chase
sections.body:
The unequivocal proof came from Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952), who worked with bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. A phage attaches to a bacterium, its genetic material enters the cell, and the cell then makes more viruses. The question was whether it was DNA or protein that entered.

Labelling. Some phages were grown on a medium containing radioactive phosphorus (32P) and some on a medium containing radioactive sulfur (35S). DNA contains phosphorus but not sulfur, so the first batch had radioactive DNA. Protein contains sulfur (in cysteine and methionine) but not phosphorus, so the second batch had radioactive protein coats.

Infection, blending, centrifugation. The radioactive phages were allowed to attach to E. coli. As infection proceeded the viral coats were removed from the bacteria by agitating them in a blender. The mixture was then centrifuged to separate the heavier bacterial cells (pellet) from the lighter viral particles (supernatant).

Result. Bacteria infected with 32P-labelled phages were radioactive, meaning DNA had entered the cells. Bacteria infected with 35S-labelled phages were not radioactive; the protein had stayed outside in the supernatant. Conclusion: DNA is the genetic material that passes from virus to bacterium; the protein coat does not.

The four-part question on this experiment (why phages, why two media, why a blender and a centrifuge, what conclusion) has appeared several times. Answer each part in one or two lines and always link 32P to DNA and 35S to protein explicitly.

formulas.expr: <sup>32</sup>P labels DNA (P present, S absent); <sup>35</sup>S labels protein (S present, P absent)
where: shears viral coats off the bacterial surface
pellets bacteria, leaves viral coats in the supernatant

sections.tip: Say that the radioactivity of <sup>32</sup>P was found in the bacterial pellet and of <sup>35</sup>S in the supernatant; naming where each label ended up is what the marking scheme checks.

sections.heading: 5.2.2 Properties of Genetic Material (DNA versus RNA) and 5.3 RNA World
sections.body:
Hershey and Chase settled the question for DNA-viruses and cells, but some viruses (tobacco mosaic virus, QB bacteriophage) use RNA as genetic material. NCERT therefore lists what any molecule must do to act as genetic material: (i) it should be able to replicate; (ii) it should be chemically and structurally stable; (iii) it should provide scope for slow changes (mutation) that evolution requires; (iv) it should be able to express itself as Mendelian characters.

Replication. Both DNA and RNA have complementary base pairing and can direct their own copying; proteins cannot. Stability. DNA wins. Its two strands, being complementary, can be separated by heat and will come back together; the 2'-OH group present in every ribose of RNA is a reactive group that makes RNA labile and easily degradable, and RNA is also catalytic and therefore reactive. In DNA, thymine replaces uracil, which gives extra stability. Mutation. Both can mutate, but RNA, being unstable, mutates faster, which is why RNA viruses have short life spans and evolve rapidly. Expression. RNA can directly code for protein synthesis; DNA depends on RNA for it. So, in NCERT's words, DNA is the better material for storage of genetic information and RNA is better for its transmission (expression). The 2-mark question 'why is DNA a better genetic material than RNA' wants stability (2'-OH absent, thymine, double strand) and slower mutation.

RNA world. RNA was the first genetic material. Essential life processes such as metabolism, translation and splicing evolved around RNA, and RNA served both as genetic material and as a catalyst (ribozymes). But being reactive it was unstable, so DNA, with chemical modifications that made it more stable, evolved from RNA, and the double-stranded form gave it resistance to change, with the second strand allowing repair. The three reasons for 'RNA was the first genetic material' are: RNA can act as genetic material (RNA viruses), RNA can act as a catalyst, and key processes still depend on RNA.

formulas.expr: Criteria of genetic material: replicate · stable · slow mutation · express itself
where: reactive group in ribose that makes RNA labile

sections.tip: The phrase 'DNA is better for storage, RNA for transmission' comes straight from NCERT; write it as the concluding line of any DNA-versus-RNA answer.

sections.heading: 5.4.1 Replication: The Experimental Proof
sections.body:
Watson and Crick's helix suggested the copying mechanism at once: the two strands separate and each acts as a template for a new complementary strand. After one round each daughter molecule has one parental strand and one new strand, so replication is semi-conservative. This is the property (complementary base pairing) that NCERT exercise 5.5 asks about.

Meselson and Stahl (1958) proved it in E. coli. They grew the bacteria in a medium whose only nitrogen source was 15NH4Cl (15N is a heavy isotope, not radioactive) for many generations, so both strands of every DNA molecule contained 15N and the DNA was heavy. They then transferred the cells to a medium with normal 14NH4Cl and took samples at definite intervals as the cells multiplied (generation time about 20 minutes). DNA extracted from each sample was centrifuged in a caesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient, which separates DNA by density. The heavy and light DNA could be distinguished because 15N-DNA and 14N-DNA form bands at different positions.

Result. DNA extracted after 20 minutes (one generation) formed a single hybrid (intermediate) density band. DNA after 40 minutes (two generations) gave equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA. This is exactly what the semi-conservative model predicts; a conservative model would have given heavy plus light after one generation, and a dispersive model would never give a purely light band. Conclusion: DNA replicates semi-conservatively, each daughter having one parental and one new strand.

Taylor and colleagues (1958) confirmed the same with radioactive thymidine in the root cells of Vicia faba (faba bean), showing that chromosomes also replicate semi-conservatively.

The 4-part question on this experiment (the nitrogen source, why heavy and light DNA were made, how they were distinguished, the conclusion) is a favourite; give the isotopes, the CsCl gradient and the 20-minute and 40-minute bands.

formulas.expr: Generation 0: heavy (<sup>15</sup>N/<sup>15</sup>N) · 20 min: all hybrid (<sup>15</sup>N/<sup>14</sup>N) · 40 min: ½ hybrid + ½ light (<sup>14</sup>N/<sup>14</sup>N) · 60 min: ¼ hybrid + ¾ light

sections.tip: Do not call <sup>15</sup>N radioactive; it is a heavy isotope. The radioactive experiment is Taylor's, with thymidine in Vicia faba.

sections.heading: 5.4.2 Replication: The Machinery and the Enzymes
sections.body:
Replication is a complex, energy-demanding process run by a set of enzymes. The main one is DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, which uses a DNA template to catalyse polymerisation of deoxynucleotides. It is fast: E. coli, with 4.6 × 106 bp, finishes replication in about 18 minutes, an average rate of about 2000 bp per second, and it is also highly accurate, since an error would be a mutation.

Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dGTP, dCTP, dTTP) play a dual role: they are the substrates for polymerisation, and their two terminal high-energy phosphates provide the energy for it. This is the 'dual purpose' the 2-mark question asks for.

The helix cannot be opened along its whole length because that would need too much energy, so it opens over a small stretch to form a replication fork, and replication proceeds as the fork moves. DNA polymerase polymerises only in the 5'→3' direction, and the two template strands are antiparallel, so replication on the two strands differs. On the template with 3'→5' polarity the new strand is made continuously (the leading strand). On the template with 5'→3' polarity it is made discontinuously, as short fragments (Okazaki fragments) that are later joined by DNA ligase. Ligase is the second enzyme the examiner expects by name.

Replication does not start anywhere: it begins at a definite region called the origin of replication (ori), which is why a foreign piece of DNA that becomes part of a chromosome can replicate only if it has, or is joined to, an origin; that is also why vectors in recombinant DNA technology need an ori. In eukaryotes replication takes place in the S phase of the cell cycle, and replication and cell division are tightly coordinated; if replication is not followed by division the cell becomes polyploid.

The 5-mark version wants the labelled fork (parental strands, 3' and 5' ends, continuous strand, discontinuous fragments, ligase, polymerase) and the roles of dNTPs, DNA polymerase and DNA ligase in words.

formulas.expr: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase: 5'→3' synthesis only; template 3'→5' → continuous strand; template 5'→3' → discontinuous fragments joined by DNA ligase
where: origin of replication, where replication begins

sections.tip: Marking schemes reward 'DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5'→3' direction' as the reason for discontinuous synthesis; write it before naming ligase.

sections.heading: 5.5 Transcription: Transcription Unit and the Gene
sections.body:
Transcription is copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA, again using complementarity, with one change: adenine now pairs with uracil. Unlike replication, only a segment of DNA and only one strand is copied. NCERT gives two reasons: if both strands were templates they would code for RNAs of different sequences, hence different proteins, complicating the transfer of information; and the two RNAs would be complementary and would pair to form double-stranded RNA, so no translation could occur.

Transcription unit. A transcription unit has three regions: a promoter, the structural gene and a terminator. Since DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase both work 5'→3', the strand with 3'→5' polarity acts as the template strand. The other strand, with 5'→3' polarity, has the same sequence as the RNA (with T in place of U) and is displaced during transcription; it is called the coding strand, and by convention all reference points on a transcription unit are given with respect to it. The promoter is a DNA sequence at the 5'-end (upstream) of the structural gene, where RNA polymerase binds; the terminator is at the 3'-end (downstream) and ends transcription. The presence of the promoter is what defines which strand is template and which is coding.

Transcription unit and the gene. A gene is the functional unit of inheritance, located on DNA. A cistron is a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide. Eukaryotic structural genes are monocistronic (one polypeptide each) and prokaryotic ones are polycistronic. In eukaryotes the coding sequence is interrupted: the coding regions, exons, appear in the mature or processed RNA, and the intervening sequences, introns, do not. Such genes are split genes. Regulatory sequences (promoter, operator) are often loosely called regulatory genes even though they do not code for RNA or protein.

A frequent 3-marker gives you one strand and asks you to construct the transcription unit or write the mRNA. Rule: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, and identical to the coding strand with U replacing T. Always mark polarity.

formulas.expr: Transcription unit = promoter (upstream, 5' of coding strand) + structural gene + terminator (downstream, 3')
where: 5'→3', same sequence as mRNA with T for U

formulas.expr: mRNA = coding strand with U in place of T; mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template strand

sections.tip: The strand that is copied is the template, but the strand named 'coding' is the one NOT copied. Students reverse this under pressure; write the polarity next to each strand and check it against the mRNA.

sections.heading: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the Process of Transcription
sections.body:
Bacteria have three major RNAs, all needed for protein synthesis: mRNA provides the template, tRNA brings amino acids and reads the genetic code, and rRNA plays structural and catalytic roles in the ribosome.

Transcription in bacteria. A single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcribes all three RNAs, in three steps. Initiation: RNA polymerase binds the promoter with the help of the initiation factor sigma (σ). Elongation: the enzyme uses nucleoside triphosphates as substrates and polymerises RNA in the 5'→3' direction, following complementarity, opening a short stretch of the helix and elongating the RNA chain; only a short stretch of RNA stays bound to the enzyme. Termination: when the polymerase reaches the terminator, the termination factor rho (ρ) causes the nascent RNA and the enzyme to fall off. RNA polymerase alone can only elongate; it is the transient association with sigma and rho that gives initiation and termination. In prokaryotes the mRNA needs no processing, and because there is no nucleus, transcription and translation take place in the same compartment and are coupled: translation can begin before transcription finishes.

Transcription in eukaryotes has two additional complexities. First, there are three RNA polymerases in the nucleus: RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S), RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), and RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs. Second, the primary transcript contains both exons and introns and is non-functional until processed. Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons in a defined order. Capping adds an unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate, to the 5' end; tailing adds 200–300 adenylate residues (the poly-A tail) to the 3' end in a template-independent manner. The fully processed hnRNA, now mRNA, is transported out of the nucleus for translation. Splicing hints at the RNA world, since the split-gene arrangement is thought to be an ancient feature of the genome.

formulas.expr: Bacteria: one RNA polymerase; σ factor → initiation; ρ factor → termination; RNA grows 5'→3'
where: transcription and translation in the same compartment

formulas.expr: Eukaryotes: RNA pol I → rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA pol II → hnRNA (mRNA); RNA pol III → tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNA

sections.tip: For 'how is transcription more complex in eukaryotes', write exactly three points: three polymerases, split genes needing splicing, and capping plus tailing. That is the full 3 marks.

sections.heading: 5.6 Genetic Code and 5.6.1 Mutations and Genetic Code
sections.body:
Replication and transcription rely on complementarity, but translation does not: the four bases of mRNA must direct the sequence of twenty amino acids. The genetic code is the set of rules that maps nucleotide triplets to amino acids. Learn the four names and their contributions, because a 3-marker asks for them. George Gamow, a physicist, argued that a code of three nucleotides is needed, since 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 triplets can cover 20 amino acids while 42 = 16 cannot. Har Gobind Khorana chemically synthesised RNA molecules of defined base combinations (homopolymers and copolymers). Marshall Nirenberg developed a cell-free system for protein synthesis. Severo Ochoa discovered the enzyme polynucleotide phosphorylase, which helped polymerise RNA with defined sequences without a template. Together these gave the checkerboard of 64 codons.

Salient features of the code. (i) It is a triplet code; 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop or termination codons. (ii) One codon codes for only one amino acid; the code is unambiguous and specific. (iii) Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon; the code is degenerate. (iv) The codons are read continuously in the mRNA, with no punctuation; the code is commaless. (v) The code is nearly universal: UUU codes for phenylalanine in bacteria and in humans, with a few exceptions in mitochondrial codons and in some protozoans. (vi) AUG has a dual function: it codes for methionine and it is the initiator codon. Only two amino acids, methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG), have a single codon.

Mutations and the code. A point mutation changes a single base pair; the NCERT example is sickle-cell anaemia, where a change in one base in the β-globin gene (GAG → GUG) replaces glutamic acid with valine. Insertion or deletion of one or two bases shifts the reading frame from that point onward, a frame-shift mutation; inserting or deleting three bases (or multiples of three) adds or removes one codon, so one amino acid changes and the rest of the frame is unchanged. NCERT's sentence 'RAM HAS RED CAP' illustrates the point: delete one letter and every word after it becomes nonsense.

formulas.expr: 4<sup>3</sup> = 64 codons = 61 sense + 3 stop (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG = Met + initiator
where: more than one codon per amino acid
one codon codes only one amino acid
only amino acids with a single codon

formulas.expr: Sickle-cell: GAG → GUG (Glu → Val) in β-globin; ±1 or ±2 bases → frame shift; ±3 bases → one codon gained or lost

sections.tip: When given an mRNA and its amino acids and asked which properties can be inferred, check: same codon → same amino acid (unambiguous), different codons → same amino acid (degenerate), a run of triplets without gaps (commaless), AUG at the start (initiator). Universality cannot be inferred from one organism's data.

sections.heading: 5.6.2 tRNA: the Adapter Molecule
sections.body:
How does a codon on mRNA specify an amino acid when the two cannot recognise each other directly? Francis Crick postulated an adapter molecule that reads the code on one side and binds a specific amino acid on the other. That molecule is tRNA (once called sRNA, soluble RNA). A tRNA has an anticodon loop carrying three bases complementary to the codon, and an amino acid acceptor end to which the amino acid is attached. tRNAs are specific for each amino acid; a codon UAC for tyrosine is read by a tRNA with anticodon AUG (written 3'→5' opposite the codon's 5'→3'), and it carries tyrosine.

Shape. The secondary structure, as drawn in NCERT, looks like a clover leaf; the actual three-dimensional structure is a compact, inverted L. In a diagram show the anticodon loop at the bottom, the two side loops, the amino acid acceptor end at the 3' end on top, the 5' end beside it, and the hydrogen-bonded stem regions.

There are no tRNAs for stop codons, which is why translation stops there. There is a special initiator tRNA for methionine at the initiation codon AUG.

Charging of tRNA (aminoacylation). Before an amino acid can be used it is activated in the presence of ATP and linked to its cognate tRNA by the enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase; this is charging. It matters because only a charged tRNA can bring the amino acid to the ribosome, and because the high-energy bond made during charging drives peptide bond formation when two charged tRNAs are brought close together. The 2-mark question 'what is aminoacylation and why is it necessary' wants both the definition (with ATP) and the reason (peptide bond formation).

formulas.expr: Codon (mRNA, 5'→3') : anticodon (tRNA, 3'→5') antiparallel and complementary; e.g. codon UAC (Tyr) ↔ anticodon AUG
where: Crick's term: reads code on one end, binds amino acid on the other
specific tRNA for Met at AUG

formulas.expr: Amino acid + ATP + tRNA → aminoacyl-tRNA (charged tRNA), catalysed by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
where: aminoacylation; its high-energy bond powers peptide bond formation

sections.tip: Draw the clover leaf, then add one line: 'the actual structure is an inverted L'. Both are asked in the same question.

sections.heading: 5.7 Translation
sections.body:
Translation is the polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide, with the order of amino acids set by the sequence of bases in mRNA. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, and forming a peptide bond needs energy. So, in the first phase, each amino acid is activated in the presence of ATP and linked to its specific tRNA, the charging of tRNA or aminoacylation. When two charged tRNAs are brought close enough, a peptide bond forms between their amino acids, and the ribosome is the cellular factory that makes this happen efficiently.

The ribosome has two subunits, a larger and a smaller one. In bacteria the ribosome is 70S (50S + 30S). In its inactive state the subunits are separate; when the smaller subunit encounters an mRNA, translation begins. The larger subunit has two sites for subsequent amino acids to come close enough for a peptide bond to form. The rRNA of the large subunit acts as the catalyst for peptide-bond formation: a ribozyme. This answers NCERT exercise 5.9 on the two essential roles of the ribosome: it provides the sites for mRNA and tRNAs to bind, and its rRNA catalyses peptide-bond formation.

Translational unit. On mRNA the sequence of RNA that is translated is flanked by the start codon AUG and one of the stop codons. The mRNA also has additional sequences that are not translated, the untranslated regions (UTRs), present at both the 5' end (before AUG) and the 3' end (after the stop codon); they are required for efficient translation.

Steps. Initiation: the ribosome binds the mRNA at the start codon AUG, which is recognised only by the initiator tRNA carrying methionine. Elongation: complexes of an amino acid with its tRNA bind to the appropriate codon on mRNA by base pairing between codon and anticodon; the ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time and the amino acids are added to the growing chain, peptide bond by peptide bond. Termination: when the ribosome reaches a stop codon, for which there is no tRNA, a release factor binds, the completed polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates from the mRNA.

formulas.expr: Translation: charging of tRNA (ATP) → initiation at AUG (initiator tRNA, Met) → elongation (codon–anticodon pairing, peptide bonds by 23S rRNA ribozyme) → termination at UAA/UAG/UGA (release factor)
where: untranslated region at 5' and 3' ends, needed for efficient translation

sections.tip: Two named non-protein players score easily: the ribozyme (rRNA of the large subunit) makes the peptide bond, and the release factor ends translation at the stop codon.

sections.heading: 5.8 Regulation of Gene Expression: the Lac Operon
sections.body:
A gene's expression is regulated at several levels. In eukaryotes NCERT lists four: (i) transcriptional level (formation of the primary transcript), (ii) processing level (splicing), (iii) transport of mRNA from nucleus to cytosol, and (iv) translational level. In prokaryotes control of the rate of transcriptional initiation is the predominant site of regulation. Genes are switched on or off in response to metabolic, physiological or environmental conditions; for example, E. coli makes the enzyme β-galactosidase to hydrolyse lactose only when lactose is present.

Transcription of a gene is regulated by accessory proteins that interact with the promoter. An operator is a sequence, usually next to the promoter, to which a repressor protein binds; each operon has its own specific operator and repressor. The operon concept was proposed by Jacob and Monod: a polycistronic structural gene regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes. Examples are the lac, trp, ara, his and val operons.

The lac operon has a regulatory gene i (inhibitor), the promoter p, the operator o and three structural genes: z codes for β-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose; y codes for permease, which increases the permeability of the cell to β-galactosides; a codes for transacetylase. All three are needed to metabolise lactose. Lactose is the inducer: it is the substrate of β-galactosidase and it regulates switching the operon on and off. It enters the cell through permease, and a very low basal level of lac operon expression is always present so that some permease exists.

Absence of inducer (switched off): the i gene is transcribed constitutively and its repressor protein binds the operator, preventing RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes. Presence of inducer (switched on): lactose binds the repressor and inactivates it, so the repressor cannot bind the operator, RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a, and the enzymes are made. Since the repressor acts by blocking transcription, this is negative regulation. (NCERT notes the lac operon is also under positive control, but that is outside the syllabus.)

NCERT exercise 5.10 asks why the operon shuts down some time after lactose is added: as β-galactosidase hydrolyses the lactose, the inducer is used up, the repressor is again free to bind the operator, and transcription stops.

formulas.expr: Lac operon: i (repressor) – p (promoter) – o (operator) – z (β-galactosidase) – y (permease) – a (transacetylase)
where: lactose; binds and inactivates the repressor
repressor blocks transcription when bound to the operator

sections.tip: In the switched-off diagram the repressor must sit on the operator, not the promoter, and RNA polymerase must be drawn at the promoter unable to move ahead. Label i, p, o, z, y, a.

sections.heading: 5.9 Human Genome Project
sections.body:
The Human Genome Project (HGP) was a 13-year mega project launched in 1990 and completed in 2003, coordinated by the US Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health, joined later by the Wellcome Trust (UK) and other countries. NCERT exercise 5.12 asks why it is called a mega project: the human genome has about 3 × 109 bp; at about 3 US dollars per base the sequencing cost would be about 9 billion US dollars; stored as typed text with 1000 letters per page and 1000 pages per book, the sequence would need 3300 books; and handling this needed new high-speed computational tools, which grew into bioinformatics.

Goals of HGP. Identify all the approximately 20,000–25,000 genes in human DNA; determine the sequences of the 3 billion chemical base pairs; store the information in databases; improve tools for data analysis; transfer related technologies to other sectors such as industry; and address the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) that arise.

Methodologies. Two approaches were used: expressed sequence tags (ESTs), which identify all genes expressed as RNA, and sequence annotation, the blind approach of sequencing the whole genome, coding and non-coding, and later assigning function. Steps: isolate the total DNA and convert it into random fragments of manageable size; clone the fragments in suitable vectors, usually bacterial artificial chromosomes (BAC) and yeast artificial chromosomes (YAC), to amplify them; sequence the fragments with automated DNA sequencers working on the principle developed by Frederick Sanger; align the overlapping sequences by computer; and prepare genetic and physical maps using microsatellite polymorphisms and RFLP markers. Genomes of many non-human organisms were also sequenced: bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, rice and Arabidopsis.

Salient features of the human genome (asked as a 3-marker): it contains 3164.7 million bases; the average gene has 3000 bases, but sizes vary, the largest known being dystrophin at 2.4 million bases; the total number of genes is about 30,000, far fewer than expected, and 99.9% of nucleotide bases are identical in all people; functions are unknown for over 50% of discovered genes; less than 2% of the genome codes for proteins; repeated sequences make up a very large portion; chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and the Y chromosome the fewest (231); about 1.4 million locations of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified, which promise to help find disease-associated sequences and trace human history.

Applications and challenges. Knowing the genome allows studies of how thousands of genes and proteins work together in the interconnected networks of a living organism, and helps in understanding disease, drug design and forensics.

formulas.expr: HGP: 1990–2003, 13 years; 3 × 10<sup>9</sup> bp; ~9 billion US dollars; 3300 books of 1000 pages × 1000 letters
where: expressed sequence tags, genes expressed as RNA
sequence whole genome, then assign functions
bacterial / yeast artificial chromosome vectors for cloning fragments

formulas.expr: Human genome: 3164.7 million bases; ~30,000 genes; avg gene 3000 bases; dystrophin 2.4 million bases; 99.9% identical; <2% codes protein; chr 1 = 2968 genes, Y = 231; 1.4 million SNPs

sections.tip: For 'two methodologies of HGP' write ESTs and sequence annotation, one line each; for BAC and YAC write both the expansion and their use as cloning vectors for DNA fragments.

sections.heading: 5.10 DNA Fingerprinting
sections.body:
Since 99.9% of the human genome is the same in everyone, telling individuals apart by sequencing would mean finding differences in the remaining 0.1%, a huge task. DNA fingerprinting is a quick way to compare DNA sequences of two individuals. It identifies differences in specific regions of the DNA called repetitive DNA, where a small stretch is repeated many times. These repeats separate as a distinct peak during density-gradient centrifugation, away from the bulk genomic DNA, and are therefore called satellite DNA. Satellite DNA is classified into micro-satellites and mini-satellites on the basis of base composition (A : T rich or G : C rich), length of the segment and number of repetitive units. These sequences do not code for proteins but form a large portion of the genome and show a high degree of polymorphism, which is the basis of fingerprinting.

Polymorphism (variation at the genetic level) arises from mutation. A mutation in a germ cell is passed to the next generation, so the variation is inheritable. Mutations in non-coding DNA accumulate over generations because they have no immediate effect on reproductive ability, which is why non-coding regions are so variable. By definition, an allele is polymorphic when it occurs in the population at a frequency of more than 0.01. DNA polymorphism is the basis of genetic mapping and of DNA fingerprinting.

The technique (Alec Jeffreys) uses a satellite DNA called VNTR (variable number of tandem repeats), a mini-satellite of 0.1 to 20 kb, whose copy number varies from person to person and from chromosome to chromosome. The steps, in NCERT order: (i) isolation of DNA; (ii) digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases; (iii) separation of fragments by gel electrophoresis; (iv) transfer (blotting) of the separated fragments to a synthetic membrane such as nitrocellulose or nylon (Southern blotting); (v) hybridisation using a labelled VNTR probe; (vi) detection of hybridised fragments by autoradiography. The autoradiogram shows bands of different sizes, and this band pattern is unique to each individual except for identical twins. Since very little DNA is usually available, the sample is now amplified by PCR first.

Applications: forensic science (matching a suspect to a crime-scene sample), paternity disputes, identification of victims (as in a train accident where bodies are burnt beyond recognition), study of genetic diversity in populations, and conservation of species. Half of a child's bands match the mother's and the rest must match the biological father's; that is how a drop of blood or a tissue sample settles paternity.

formulas.expr: DNA fingerprinting: isolate DNA → restriction digestion → gel electrophoresis → Southern blotting to nylon/nitrocellulose → hybridise with labelled VNTR probe → autoradiography
where: variable number of tandem repeats; mini-satellite, 0.1–20 kb
repetitive DNA that forms a separate peak in density-gradient centrifugation

sections.tip: The probe is a labelled VNTR sequence and the detection step is autoradiography; students who write 'observe the bands under UV' lose the last mark.

key_terms.definition: A nitrogenous base linked to the 1' carbon of a pentose sugar through an N-glycosidic linkage; adding a phosphate at the 5'-OH gives a nucleotide.
The 3'-5' bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next; it forms the sugar-phosphate backbone of a polynucleotide chain.
In double-stranded DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine, so A : T = G : C = 1 and purines equal pyrimidines.
The unit of eukaryotic DNA packaging: about 200 bp of negatively charged DNA wrapped around a positively charged histone octamer, with H1 at the entry and exit points.
Loosely packed, lightly stained chromatin that is transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is densely packed, dark and inactive.
Griffith's name for the factor from heat-killed S-strain Streptococcus pneumoniae that made live R cells virulent; Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed it is DNA.
Each daughter DNA molecule retains one parental strand and receives one newly synthesised strand; proven by Meselson and Stahl using 15N in E. coli.
The definite region of DNA where replication begins; a foreign DNA can replicate in a cell only if it carries or is joined to such an origin.
The enzyme that joins the discontinuously synthesised fragments of the lagging strand during replication (and DNA fragments in recombinant DNA work).
In a transcription unit the 3'→5' strand is the template copied by RNA polymerase; the 5'→3' strand, which has the mRNA sequence with T for U, is the coding strand.
A segment of DNA that codes for one polypeptide; eukaryotic structural genes are monocistronic and prokaryotic genes are polycistronic.
Exons are the expressed coding sequences of a split gene that appear in mature RNA; introns are intervening sequences removed during splicing.
Heterogeneous nuclear RNA, the primary transcript of RNA polymerase II in eukaryotes, which becomes mRNA after splicing, capping and tailing.
Sigma is the initiation factor and rho the termination factor that associate transiently with bacterial RNA polymerase, which on its own can only elongate.
The property that most amino acids are coded by more than one codon; only methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG) have a single codon.
Insertion or deletion of one or two bases that shifts the reading frame from that point onward, changing every codon downstream.
Charging: activation of an amino acid using ATP and its attachment to its specific tRNA by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase; the high-energy bond later drives peptide bond formation.
An RNA that acts as an enzyme; the rRNA of the large ribosomal subunit catalyses peptide bond formation during translation.
A polycistronic structural gene regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes, as in the lac, trp, ara, his and val operons; proposed by Jacob and Monod.
A small molecule that binds and inactivates the repressor so the operon is switched on; lactose is the inducer of the lac operon.
One of the two HGP methods: identifying all the genes that are expressed as RNA, as opposed to sequence annotation of the whole genome.
A single-base variation in the genome; about 1.4 million SNP locations were found in the human genome and help locate disease-associated sequences.
Variable number of tandem repeats: a mini-satellite DNA of 0.1–20 kb whose copy number varies between individuals; the labelled VNTR is the probe in DNA fingerprinting.
Repetitive DNA that separates as a distinct peak from bulk genomic DNA in density-gradient centrifugation; classified into micro- and mini-satellites.

ncert_questions.q: Group the following as nitrogenous bases and nucleosides: Adenine, Cytidine, Thymine, Guanosine, Uracil and Cytosine.
ncert_questions.a:
Nitrogenous bases: Adenine, Thymine, Uracil, Cytosine.

Nucleosides: Cytidine (cytosine + ribose), Guanosine (guanine + ribose).

A nucleoside is a base attached to a pentose sugar by an N-glycosidic linkage; the names ending in -sine or -dine (adenosine, guanosine, cytidine, uridine) are nucleosides, while adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil are the bases.

ncert_questions.q: If a double stranded DNA has 20 per cent of cytosine, calculate the per cent of adenine in the DNA.
ncert_questions.a:
By Chargaff's rule, in double-stranded DNA G = C and A = T.

C = 20%, so G = 20%. G + C = 40%.

A + T = 100% − 40% = 60%, and since A = T, A = 60/2 = 30%.

Check: A (30) + T (30) + G (20) + C (20) = 100%.

ncert_questions.q: If the sequence of one strand of DNA is written as follows: 5'-ATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGC-3', write down the sequence of the complementary strand in 5'→3' direction.
ncert_questions.a:
The complementary strand is antiparallel, so write it first 3'→5' by pairing A with T and G with C:

3'-TACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACG-5'

Then read it in the 5'→3' direction (reverse it):

5'-GCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCAT-3'

Check the first base: the 3' end of the given strand is C, so the 5' end of the complementary strand must be G, which it is.

ncert_questions.q: If the sequence of the coding strand in a transcription unit is written as follows: 5'-ATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGC-3', write down the sequence of mRNA.
ncert_questions.a:
The mRNA has the same sequence and polarity as the coding strand, with uracil in place of thymine (the template strand, not the coding strand, is copied).

5'-AUGCAUGCAUGCAUGCAUGCAUGCAUGC-3'

Note that the mRNA begins with AUG, the initiator codon.

ncert_questions.q: Which property of DNA double helix led Watson and Crick to hypothesise semi-conservative mode of DNA replication? Explain.
ncert_questions.a: The property is complementary base pairing between the two strands (A with T, G with C). Because each strand carries the information to specify the other, Watson and Crick proposed that during replication the two strands separate and each acts as a template for the synthesis of a new complementary strand. The result is two DNA molecules, each with one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand, which is the semi-conservative mode of replication. This was later proved experimentally by Meselson and Stahl (1958).

ncert_questions.q: Depending upon the chemical nature of the template (DNA or RNA) and the type of nucleic acids synthesised from it (DNA or RNA), list the types of nucleic acid polymerases.
ncert_questions.a:
1. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase: DNA template, synthesises DNA (replication).
  2. DNA-dependent RNA polymerase: DNA template, synthesises RNA (transcription).
  3. RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase): RNA template, synthesises DNA (in retroviruses).
  4. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RNA replicase): RNA template, synthesises RNA (in RNA viruses).

ncert_questions.q: How did Hershey and Chase differentiate between DNA and protein in their experiment while proving that DNA is the genetic material?
ncert_questions.a: They used radioactive isotopes that label only one of the two molecules. Bacteriophages grown in a medium with radioactive phosphorus (32P) had labelled DNA, because DNA contains phosphorus but protein does not. Phages grown in a medium with radioactive sulfur (35S) had labelled protein coats, because protein contains sulfur (in cysteine and methionine) while DNA does not. After infection of E. coli, the coats were removed by blending and the bacteria pelleted by centrifugation. Radioactivity of 32P was found inside the bacteria and that of 35S stayed outside in the supernatant, showing that DNA, not protein, had entered the bacteria and is the genetic material.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between the following: (a) Repetitive DNA and Satellite DNA (b) mRNA and tRNA (c) Template strand and Coding strand.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Repetitive DNA is any DNA in which a small stretch of sequence is repeated many times; satellite DNA is that fraction of repetitive DNA which separates from bulk genomic DNA as a distinct peak (satellite) in density-gradient centrifugation, and is classified into micro- and mini-satellites.

(b) mRNA is a linear molecule that carries the genetic information from DNA to the ribosome and acts as the template for translation; tRNA is a clover-leaf shaped (inverted L in 3D) adapter molecule that carries a specific amino acid at its acceptor end and reads the codon through its anticodon loop.

(c) The template strand has 3'→5' polarity and is the strand actually copied by RNA polymerase into RNA; the coding strand has 5'→3' polarity, is not transcribed, and has the same sequence as the RNA (with T in place of U).

ncert_questions.q: List two essential roles of ribosome during translation.
ncert_questions.a:
1. The ribosome provides the sites at which the mRNA and the charged tRNAs bind: the small subunit binds mRNA, and the large subunit has two sites that hold successive aminoacyl-tRNAs close enough for a peptide bond to form.
  2. The rRNA of the large subunit acts as a ribozyme that catalyses the formation of the peptide bond between amino acids.

ncert_questions.q: In the medium where E. coli was growing, lactose was added, which induced the lac operon. Then, why does lac operon shut down some time after addition of lactose in the medium?
ncert_questions.a: Lactose is the inducer of the lac operon. When added, it binds the repressor protein (product of the i gene) and inactivates it, so the repressor cannot bind the operator, RNA polymerase transcribes the z, y and a genes, and β-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase are made. β-galactosidase then hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose. As the lactose is consumed, the inducer concentration falls, the repressor is again free and active, binds the operator, and transcription of the structural genes stops. The operon is switched off because its own product removes the inducer.

ncert_questions.q: Explain (in one or two lines) the function of the following: (a) Promoter (b) tRNA (c) Exons.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Promoter: a DNA sequence at the 5' end (upstream) of the structural gene that provides the binding site for RNA polymerase and thereby defines the template and coding strands of the transcription unit.

(b) tRNA: the adapter molecule that carries a specific amino acid to the ribosome and reads the codon on mRNA through its anticodon during translation.

(c) Exons: the coding or expressed sequences of a eukaryotic (split) gene that remain after splicing and appear in the mature mRNA.

ncert_questions.q: Why is the Human Genome Project called a mega project?
ncert_questions.a:
• The human genome contains about 3 × 109 base pairs; sequencing at about 3 US dollars per base would cost about 9 billion US dollars.
  • Printed at 1000 letters per page in books of 1000 pages, the sequence would fill 3300 books.
  • It took 13 years (1990–2003) and needed international coordination between many laboratories and countries.
  • It generated an enormous amount of data that required new high-speed computational devices for storage, retrieval and analysis, giving rise to bioinformatics.

ncert_questions.q: What is DNA fingerprinting? Mention its application.
ncert_questions.a:
DNA fingerprinting is a technique, developed by Alec Jeffreys, of identifying an individual by comparing the pattern of variable number of tandem repeats (VNTRs) in the repetitive (satellite) DNA of the genome. The DNA is isolated, cut with restriction endonucleases, the fragments separated by gel electrophoresis, blotted onto a nylon or nitrocellulose membrane, hybridised with a labelled VNTR probe and detected by autoradiography; the band pattern is unique to each individual (except identical twins).

Applications: forensic identification of criminals from blood, semen, hair or saliva; settling paternity disputes; identifying victims in disasters; studying genetic diversity of populations and evolutionary relationships; conservation of species.

pyq.answer: b

the supernatant, because it labelled the protein coat
the bacterial pellet, because it labelled the protein coat

pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: AUG codes for methionine and is the initiator codon; UGG is tryptophan; UAA and UGA are stop codons.

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Sigma initiates transcription, rho terminates it; the release factor acts in translation.

pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: z codes for β-galactosidase, y for permease, a for transacetylase and i for the repressor.

pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The variable number of tandem repeats (a mini-satellite) is the polymorphic sequence that the labelled probe hybridises to on the blot.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): DNA is a better genetic material than RNA for storing genetic information. Reason (R): The 2'-OH group present in every nucleotide of RNA makes it reactive and easily degradable.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: RNA's 2'-OH makes it labile, so DNA, lacking it and having thymine and a complementary second strand, is chemically more stable and better for storage.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): During replication one strand is synthesised continuously and the other discontinuously. Reason (R): DNA-dependent DNA polymerase can polymerise nucleotides only in the 5'→3' direction and the two template strands are antiparallel.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because synthesis is only 5'→3', the 3'→5' template is copied continuously toward the fork and the 5'→3' template in fragments away from it.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Regulation of the lac operon by the repressor is called negative regulation. Reason (R): Lactose binds to the operator and switches the operon on.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The repressor blocks transcription when bound to the operator, so it is negative regulation; but lactose binds and inactivates the repressor, not the operator.

pyq.q: Write the dual purpose served by deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates in polymerisation during DNA replication.
pyq.answer:
(i) They act as the substrates for polymerisation: dATP, dGTP, dCTP and dTTP are the monomers added by DNA-dependent DNA polymerase to the growing strand.

(ii) They provide the energy for polymerisation: the two terminal phosphates are high-energy phosphates, released as pyrophosphate when the nucleotide is added.

pyq.q: Describe the structure of a nucleosome. Where is it found in a cell?
pyq.answer:
A nucleosome consists of a histone octamer (two molecules each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4), which is positively charged because histones are rich in lysine and arginine, around which about 200 bp of negatively charged DNA is wrapped. Histone H1 is present at the point where DNA enters and leaves the core. Nucleosomes repeat along the DNA to give the beads-on-string appearance of chromatin.

It is found in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, as the basic unit of chromatin.

pyq.q: Why does hnRNA undergo splicing? Where does splicing occur in the cell?
pyq.answer:
The primary transcript hnRNA, made by RNA polymerase II from a split gene, contains both exons (coding sequences) and introns (non-coding intervening sequences), so it is non-functional. Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons in a defined order so that a continuous coding sequence, the functional mRNA, is produced.

Splicing occurs inside the nucleus, along with capping and tailing, before the mRNA is transported to the cytoplasm.

pyq.q: Differentiate between a template strand and a coding strand of DNA. Name the source of energy for the replication of DNA.
pyq.answer:
Template strand: has 3'→5' polarity; it is the strand that RNA polymerase copies during transcription. Coding strand: has 5'→3' polarity; it is not transcribed but has the same sequence as the mRNA (with T in place of U).

The energy for replication comes from the deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates themselves, whose two terminal high-energy phosphates are released during polymerisation.

pyq.q: What is an origin of replication in a chromosome? State its function.
pyq.answer:
The origin of replication (ori) is a definite region of DNA at which replication is initiated.

Function: it is where the helix first opens to form a replication fork and where the replication machinery assembles; replication cannot begin anywhere else. That is why a foreign DNA can replicate in a host cell only if it carries or is joined to an origin of replication, and why vectors in recombinant DNA technology must have an ori.

pyq.q: Answer the following questions based on Meselson and Stahl's experiment on E. coli. (i) Name the chemical substance used as the only source of nitrogen in the experiment. (ii) Why did they allow the synthesis of the light and the heavy DNA molecules in the organism? (iii) How did they distinguish the heavy DNA molecules from the light DNA molecules? (iv) Write the conclusion the scientists arrived at at the end of the experiment.
pyq.answer:
(i) 15NH4Cl (ammonium chloride containing the heavy isotope 15N), later replaced by 14NH4Cl.

(ii) Growing the bacteria for many generations in 15N made all their DNA heavy; transferring them to 14N meant that any newly synthesised strand would be light. This let them follow which strands in the daughter DNA were old (heavy) and which were new (light) after each generation (20 minutes).

(iii) By centrifuging the extracted DNA in a caesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient, in which heavy (15N/15N), hybrid (15N/14N) and light (14N/14N) DNA settle at different positions. After 20 minutes only a hybrid band appeared; after 40 minutes equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA.

(iv) DNA replication is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule has one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand.

pyq.q: Answer the following questions based on Hershey and Chase's experiment. (i) Name the kind of virus they worked with and why. (ii) Why did they use two types of culture media to grow viruses? (iii) What was the need for using a blender and later a centrifuge during their experiment? (iv) State the conclusion drawn by them.
pyq.answer:
(i) Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. They inject only their genetic material into the bacterium and leave the coat outside, so the experiment could tell whether DNA or protein entered.

(ii) One medium contained radioactive phosphorus (32P), which labels only DNA, and the other radioactive sulfur (35S), which labels only protein. This allowed DNA and protein to be tracked separately.

(iii) The blender agitated the infected bacteria so that the viral coats attached to the surface were shaken off; the centrifuge then separated the heavier bacterial cells (pellet) from the lighter viral particles (supernatant), so radioactivity could be measured in each.

(iv) Bacteria infected with 32P-phages were radioactive and those infected with 35S-phages were not; hence DNA, not protein, is the genetic material that passes from virus to bacterium.

pyq.q: Following are the features of genetic codes. What does each one indicate? Stop codon, Unambiguous codon, Degenerate codon, Universal codon.
pyq.answer:
Stop codon: UAA, UAG and UGA do not code for any amino acid and have no tRNA; they signal termination of translation.

Unambiguous codon: one codon specifies only one particular amino acid and never any other; the code is specific.

Degenerate codon: the same amino acid can be coded by more than one codon (for example, several codons for leucine or serine); the code is degenerate.

Universal codon: a given codon specifies the same amino acid in all organisms from bacteria to humans (UUU is phenylalanine in both), with a few exceptions in mitochondrial codons and some protozoans.

pyq.q: Describe how the lac operon operates, both in the presence and the absence of an inducer in E. coli.
pyq.answer:
The lac operon consists of the regulatory gene i, the promoter p, the operator o and the structural genes z (β-galactosidase), y (permease) and a (transacetylase). Lactose is the inducer.

In the absence of the inducer (no lactose): the i gene is transcribed and translated into the repressor protein. The repressor binds to the operator, which prevents RNA polymerase, bound at the promoter, from transcribing the structural genes. The operon is switched off and no lactose-metabolising enzymes are made.

In the presence of the inducer: lactose enters the cell through the small amount of permease always present and binds the repressor, inactivating it. The inactive repressor cannot bind the operator, so RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a into a polycistronic mRNA and the three enzymes are produced; β-galactosidase hydrolyses lactose to glucose and galactose. As the repressor blocks transcription, this is negative regulation.

pyq.q: Write the contributions of the following scientists in deciphering the genetic code: George Gamow, Har Gobind Khorana, Marshall Nirenberg, Severo Ochoa. State the importance of the genetic code in protein biosynthesis.
pyq.answer:
George Gamow: a physicist who argued that since there are only four bases and twenty amino acids, the code must consist of three nucleotides, giving 43 = 64 codons.

Har Gobind Khorana: developed the chemical method of synthesising RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases (homopolymers and copolymers), which helped assign codons.

Marshall Nirenberg: developed the cell-free system for protein synthesis, which allowed synthetic RNAs to be translated and the code to be read.

Severo Ochoa: discovered the enzyme polynucleotide phosphorylase, which polymerises RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner.

Importance: the genetic code specifies which amino acid each mRNA triplet stands for, so it determines the sequence of amino acids, and therefore the structure and function, of every protein made during translation.

pyq.q: (i) Explain with the help of Griffith's experiment how the search for genetic material was conducted and what conclusion was drawn. (ii) How did Avery, MacLeod and McCarty establish the biochemical nature of the so-called genetic material identified by Griffith?
pyq.answer:
(i) Griffith's experiment (1928) with Streptococcus pneumoniae, which has two strains: S (smooth), with a mucous polysaccharide coat, virulent; and R (rough), without the coat, non-virulent.

  • Live S cells injected into mice → mice died of pneumonia.
  • Live R cells injected → mice survived.
  • Heat-killed S cells injected → mice survived.
  • Heat-killed S cells mixed with live R cells injected → mice died, and living S cells were recovered from the dead mice.

Conclusion: some transforming principle from the heat-killed S cells had passed into the R cells and enabled them to synthesise the smooth polysaccharide coat and become virulent. The R cells had been transformed; the chemical nature of the transforming principle was not known.

(ii) Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933–44) purified biochemicals (proteins, DNA, RNA) from heat-killed S cells and tested which could transform live R cells into S cells. Purified DNA alone caused transformation. Treatment with proteases and RNases did not affect transformation, so the principle was neither protein nor RNA; treatment with DNase inhibited transformation, showing that DNA caused it. They concluded that DNA is the hereditary material.

pyq.q: Explain the mechanism of DNA replication with the help of a labelled replication fork. What role does the enzyme DNA ligase play in a replication fork?
pyq.answer:
Diagram: a Y-shaped fork with the parental helix on the left opening into two template strands, the upper labelled 3'→5' with a continuous new strand growing 5'→3' toward the fork, the lower labelled 5'→3' with short fragments growing 5'→3' away from the fork and DNA ligase shown joining them; label DNA polymerase, direction of fork movement, leading and lagging strands.

Mechanism:

  1. Replication begins at a definite region, the origin of replication, in the S phase of the cell cycle.
  2. The two strands separate over a small stretch, since unwinding the whole helix would need too much energy, forming the replication fork; the fork moves as replication proceeds.
  3. Each separated strand acts as a template; new nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing (A with T, G with C).
  4. Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve both as substrates and as the energy source, their two terminal high-energy phosphates being released.
  5. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase polymerises nucleotides only in the 5'→3' direction. On the template with 3'→5' polarity synthesis is continuous (leading strand); on the template with 5'→3' polarity it is discontinuous, in short fragments (lagging strand).
  6. The result is two DNA molecules, each with one parental and one new strand: semi-conservative replication.

Role of DNA ligase: it joins the discontinuously synthesised fragments of the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds between them, giving one continuous strand.

pyq.q: Explain the process of transcription in prokaryotes. How is the process different in eukaryotes?
pyq.answer:
Transcription in prokaryotes is carried out by a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase on a transcription unit made of a promoter, a structural gene and a terminator. The 3'→5' strand is the template and the 5'→3' strand the coding strand.

  1. Initiation: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter with the help of the initiation factor sigma (σ).
  2. Elongation: the enzyme opens a short stretch of the helix and polymerises ribonucleoside triphosphates in the 5'→3' direction, complementary to the template (A pairs with U); the RNA chain grows while only a short stretch remains bound to the enzyme.
  3. Termination: on reaching the terminator, the termination factor rho (ρ) causes the RNA polymerase and the nascent RNA to fall off the DNA.

Prokaryotic mRNA needs no processing and, because there is no nucleus, transcription and translation are coupled in the same compartment.

Differences in eukaryotes:

  1. There are three RNA polymerases: RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA polymerase II transcribes hnRNA, the precursor of mRNA; RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs.
  2. Genes are split: the primary transcript (hnRNA) contains exons and introns and must undergo splicing, in which introns are removed and exons joined in a defined order.
  3. The hnRNA is further processed by capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate added to the 5' end) and tailing (200–300 adenylate residues added to the 3' end); only the fully processed mRNA is transported out of the nucleus for translation, so transcription and translation are not coupled.

pyq.q:
A forensic laboratory received blood samples from a crime scene and from three suspects. DNA was isolated from each, cut with a restriction endonuclease, run on a gel, blotted onto a nylon membrane, hybridised with a radioactive VNTR probe and exposed to X-ray film. The autoradiogram showed that the band pattern of suspect 2 matched the crime-scene sample exactly, while suspects 1 and 3 shared only a few bands with it.
(i) Name the technique and the scientist who developed it.
(ii) What is a VNTR and why is it chosen as the probe?
(iii) Name the step in which the fragments are transferred to the nylon membrane and the step in which the bands are finally seen.
(iv) Give one reason why suspects 1 and 3 share a few bands with the sample even though they are not the source.
pyq.answer:
(i) DNA fingerprinting, developed by Alec Jeffreys.

(ii) VNTR, variable number of tandem repeats, is a mini-satellite DNA (0.1–20 kb) made of short sequences repeated in tandem; the number of repeats varies from person to person and chromosome to chromosome, so it is highly polymorphic and gives a band pattern unique to each individual.

(iii) Transfer to the membrane is Southern blotting; the bands are seen by autoradiography.

(iv) Since 99.9% of the human genome is common to all people, and some VNTR alleles are widespread in the population, unrelated individuals will share some bands; only the complete pattern is unique (identical twins excepted).

pyq.q:
A segment of mRNA and the polypeptide it produces are given below.
5'-AUG UUU UUC GAG UUA GUG UAA-3'
Met – Phe – Phe – Glu – Leu – Val
(i) Which property of the genetic code is shown by UUU and UUC both giving phenylalanine?
(ii) Why does the polypeptide end after valine although UAA is present on the mRNA?
(iii) Which property of the code does the first codon AUG illustrate?
(iv) If the base G is deleted from the fourth codon GAG, what type of mutation results and what happens to the codons downstream?
pyq.answer:
(i) Degeneracy: more than one codon can code for the same amino acid.

(ii) UAA is a stop (termination) codon; there is no tRNA for it, so a release factor binds and the polypeptide is released.

(iii) AUG has a dual function: it codes for methionine and also acts as the initiator codon, so translation begins there.

(iv) Deleting one base causes a frame-shift mutation. The reading frame shifts by one base from that point, so every codon downstream (AGU UAG UGU AA...) is read differently; here the new frame even produces a premature stop codon UAG, so the polypeptide changes completely and is shortened.

pyq.q: Name the transcriptionally active region of chromatin in a nucleus. How does it differ from the other region?
pyq.answer:
The transcriptionally active region is euchromatin: it is loosely packed and stains light.

The other region, heterochromatin, is densely packed, stains dark and is transcriptionally inactive.

add one amino acid without altering the downstream frame

practice_mcq.explanation: Blotting moves the fragments to a membrane where they can be hybridised with the labelled VNTR probe and then detected by autoradiography.

practice_mcq.explanation: Mutations in non-coding sequences have no immediate effect on reproductive ability, so they accumulate over generations and make these regions highly variable.

common_mistakes: Reversing template and coding strands: the template (3'→5') is the one copied, the coding strand (5'→3') is the one that matches the mRNA. Examiners check the polarity you write next to each strand.
Calling 15N radioactive in Meselson and Stahl's experiment. It is a heavy isotope separated by density in a CsCl gradient; the radioactive experiment is Taylor's with thymidine in Vicia faba.

Writing that the inducer (lactose) binds the operator. Lactose binds and inactivates the repressor; the repressor is what binds the operator. In the switched-off diagram the repressor must sit on o, not on p.
Answering 'why is DNA a better genetic material' with only 'DNA is double stranded'. The scheme wants the 2'-OH of RNA making it reactive, thymine in place of uracil, and slower mutation of DNA.
Giving only two of the three eukaryotic complexities in transcription. Write three polymerases, splicing of split genes, and capping plus tailing, and name RNA polymerase II for hnRNA.
Mixing up the enzyme names: DNA ligase joins the lagging-strand fragments, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides, sigma initiates and rho terminates transcription, release factor terminates translation.
Calculating base percentages with A = G instead of A = T. First find the partner of the given base, subtract the pair from 100, then halve the remainder.

Stopping the DNA fingerprinting answer at electrophoresis. The full sequence ends with blotting to a membrane, hybridisation with a labelled VNTR probe and autoradiography; each step is a marking point.

Attributing the wrong contribution: Gamow proposed the triplet code, Nirenberg the cell-free system, Khorana synthetic RNAs, Ochoa polynucleotide phosphorylase, Jacob and Monod the operon, Jeffreys the fingerprinting technique.
strategy:
Treat this chapter as five stories, each worth a 3- or 5-mark question, and prepare each with its diagram: (1) structure and packaging of DNA, with the polynucleotide chain and nucleosome; (2) the search for genetic material, with Griffith, Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase; (3) replication, with Meselson–Stahl and the labelled fork; (4) transcription and translation, with the transcription unit, hnRNA processing, the tRNA clover leaf and the ribosome; (5) regulation and applications, with the lac operon in both states, HGP facts and the DNA fingerprinting flow chart.

Memorise the numbers on the formula sheet in one sitting: genome sizes, helix dimensions, 64/61/3 codons, the polymerases and factors, the lac operon map, the HGP figures. They feed the 1-mark and 2-mark questions and the case studies. Practise the three calculation types until they take under a minute: base percentages, complementary strand in 5'→3' form, and mRNA from a coding or template strand.

For the long answers, write from the experiments and mechanisms as numbered steps with the enzyme or factor named at each step, and draw the diagram before the text so that the labels do the explaining. The features of the genetic code and the differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic transcription should be practised as fixed lists, since the marking scheme awards a mark per point. Give two full sessions to this chapter before the exam: one for stories 1 to 3 and one for 4 and 5, each ending with a written 5-mark answer against the clock.
